lessons.title: Dress Up the Resume: What CSS Is, Its Rules and Its Three Types

objectives.cognitive: Describe what CSS does, the parts of a CSS rule and the three places CSS can be written.
objectives.affective: Value readable, consistent styling that respects every reader.
objectives.psychomotor: Write Juan's first internal and inline CSS rules in CodeShare and run them.

blocks.markdown: **How to use this module:** Work in order, Monday to Friday. Run every sample unchanged first, then do its small task. Answer each day's exit slip after its last step.

**Everything happens in CodeShare.** Open your class, then **Module**, this week and a step. **Work in code editor** loads the step's sample files into the editor tabs; **Run code** shows the step's run page in the page window and checks it, and its links open the project's other pages there. It works online and from the classroom laptop; no internet, installation, download or account is needed.

**Reading the outputs:** an output box shows the page text CodeShare checks for the step's run page: the Tab title, the Visible page text, then, on Steps 1, 3 and 9, Media checks. Colours, fonts, sizes and backgrounds are not page text; CodeShare checks them with page checks. CSS that changes letters (text-transform) or hides an element (display: none) does change the page text. Spaces count.

**Where we start:** Juan's finished Week 3 site carries forward in your module project: index.html, projects.html and contact.html. This week adds styles.css. Each step loads its run page and every file that page needs, even when unchanged; the boxes show only the lines a step adds or changes, and where they go.
**Week 4 starts here:** Juan's site has words, lists, a picture, tables, links and a form, but every page shows the browser's plain black text in its default font.

CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) sets how HTML elements look: colours, fonts, sizes and spacing. HTML says what the content is; CSS says how it looks. A rule is a selector and a declaration block: h1 { color: #13305c; }. Each declaration is a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon. CSS can be written in three places: inline (a style attribute on one element), internal (a style element in head) or external (a .css file the page links). A selector can name an element (h2), a class (.badge) or an id (#form-note).

A school uniform rule names who it is for (Grade 11 students: the selector) and what they wear (white polo: a property and its value). A note pinned to one student is inline; a rule posted in one classroom is internal; the school handbook every room follows is external.

rows: A style attribute on one element
What to change, and its new setting; # and six digits name a colour
The colon joins a property to its value; the semicolon ends each declaration

blocks.markdown: **Media steps:** Steps 1, 3 and 9 run index.html, with Juan's picture, sound and video, files your teacher adds under Media files. Online, CodeShare checks them automatically; Run code waits on Loading media… until they are on this device. Offline, these three steps show Checked by your teacher for now, and your teacher presses Mark done. Steps 2 and 4 to 8 run projects.html or contact.html and are checked automatically.

blocks.instruction: Juan's Week 3 site carries forward. This step gives index.html its first CSS: an internal style sheet, a style element in head with three rules. Each rule names a selector (body, h1, h2) and, in braces, a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon. Run it unchanged: Juan's name turns navy, the headings maroon and the font changes.

lessons.title: Inline, Internal, External: Moving Juan's Styles into One Stylesheet

objectives.cognitive: Explain which rule wins when inline, internal and external CSS set the same property.
objectives.affective: Appreciate one tidy shared stylesheet that classmates can read and change.
objectives.psychomotor: Move Juan's rules into styles.css and link it from all three pages.

blocks.markdown: **Today's starting point:** Monday's styles stay where they were written: the style element styles only index.html, and the inline style only one sentence.

When two rules give one element different values for the same property, an inline style wins over rules in a style element or a stylesheet. Between two rules of the same kind, the later one wins, so the order of the style element and the link line matters. An external stylesheet is one .css file; each page links it with a link element in head: rel="stylesheet" and href="styles.css", each value in quotes.
A class adviser's instruction to one student beats the rule posted in the room, and a newer memo on the same topic replaces an older one.

columns: When two rules set the same property on one element
rows: An inline style and a rule in a style element or stylesheet
Two rules of the same kind, for example two h1 rules
A style element after the link line, both with an h1 rule
The link line after a style element, both with an h1 rule

lessons.title: Pick Exactly What to Style: Class and ID Selectors

objectives.cognitive: Distinguish element, class and ID selectors and tell which one wins on the same element.
objectives.affective: Choose class and id names that say what they mean.
objectives.psychomotor: Style Juan's project badges with a class and his contact note with an ID.

blocks.markdown: **Today's starting point:** Element selectors style every h1 or every nav. Juan wants to style only some elements: two project badges, one sentence.

A class selector starts with a dot: .badge matches every element with class="badge", and many elements may share a class. An ID selector starts with #: #form-note matches the one element with id="form-note"; an id is used only once on a page. Class and id names are case-sensitive. On one element an ID rule beats a class rule, and a class rule beats an element rule.

At a school program, "Grade 11, stand" calls every student in the grade (an element), "Science club members, stand" calls a group that can be anywhere (a class), and "the student in seat 12, stand" calls one person (an id).

columns: On one element, these rules set its colour
rows: The style attribute: inline beats an ID

blocks.instruction: A class selector starts with a dot and matches every element with that class. This step adds a .badge rule to styles.css and gives two span elements class="badge", one after each project. Run it unchanged: both badges are small, yellow and in capitals.

blocks.markdown: **Today's starting point:** Browsers show no error for a broken CSS rule: the rule just does not apply, and part of the page looks plain again.

A browser skips any declaration it cannot read and shows no error. A missing semicolon joins two declarations into one unreadable declaration, so both are skipped; a missing colon loses that one declaration; a missing closing brace can stop every rule after it. A selector that does not match the HTML exactly (a misspelt class, a wrong capital letter, a missing dot) styles nothing.
A text message with a missing period runs two sentences together and the reader skips both; a misspelt name reaches nobody. A missing semicolon or a misspelt class does the same to a rule.

performanceTask.title: My Resume, Week 4: My Own Stylesheet
performanceTask.markdown:
Start Thursday; finish and present Friday. In CodeShare open Projects, then Personal performance-task project. Your Week 3 site carries forward: add this week's parts to it.

Add styles.css with ＋ (Create a new file) and link it from every page with a link element in head: rel="stylesheet" and href="styles.css", each value in quotes. Write element, class and ID rules there, following the requirements below, with a comment above each rule that names its type. Use only colours and fonts already on the computer: no pictures or fonts named inside CSS.

Use only safe details: no home address, phone number, birth date, ID numbers or personal social-media accounts. Run code until index.html runs with no error, visit every page with your links, then press Submit this version. Saving or running is not submitting. Pictures, sound and video stay online only (Media files).

Thursday: 0–60 minutes, repairs and the Thursday strip; 60–120 minutes, plan on paper, show the teacher, then start. Friday: 0–30 minutes, finish and run; 30–105 minutes, five-minute presentations; 105–120 minutes, Friday strip and Submit this version.
checklist: Keep your Week 3 site: every page, the navigation bar, the frame and the form.
Add styles.css with ＋ Create a new file; the name is exactly styles.css.
In head of every page, add the link element with rel="stylesheet" and href="styles.css", in quotes.
Write at least three element rules, for example body, h1 and nav, with colours that are easy to read.
Write one class rule and give that class to at least two elements.
Write one ID rule and give that id to exactly one element.
Above each rule, write a comment that names its type: element, class or ID selector.
Use only colours and fonts already on the computer; nothing named in CSS url().
No home address, phone number, birth date, ID numbers or social media.
Run code shows no error; visit every page; press Submit this version, then present and explain inline, internal and external CSS.
